claims.text: Wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by nanostructural grain-boundary stabilization.
Grain-boundary stabilization enables adaptive accommodation of local plastic deformation.
Adaptive accommodation of local plastic deformation reduces wear rate.
Adaptive accommodation of local plastic deformation reduces crack propagation.
The baseline coating has a coarse-grained microstructure with relatively low grain-boundary density.
Severe plastic deformation, such as high-energy shot peening or cold rolling, can refine the coating into a nanocrystalline regime.
Nanocrystalline grain refinement increases grain-boundary density.
The increased grain-boundary density impedes dislocation motion.
The increased grain-boundary density impedes crack propagation.
Refined grain boundaries enhance localized plastic flow during wear.
Localized plastic flow reduces crack initiation and propagation.
Refined grain boundaries provide a self-adaptive response to mechanical stress during wear.
Under equivalent wear-test conditions, nanocrystalline HEA coatings will have significantly lower wear rates than coarse-grained coatings.
Under equivalent wear-test conditions, nanocrystalline HEA coatings will exhibit delayed crack growth relative to coarse-grained coatings.
The proposed mechanism should apply across typical wear-resistant HEA coating compositions when high-temperature oxidation, phase transformations, and other competing phenomena are absent.
